doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Working with Aretha Franklin and Steely Dan
summary: He loved Aretha but found her personal side hard, found Steely Dan demanding but fine, and says he does the job and leaves.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Let me ask you about a couple — obviously we can’t talk about everybody you’ve played with, but the years spent with Aretha. What was it like?

To me it was great years. I had more problems than a barrel of monkeys on the personal side but that’s what I had to learn to live with. Aretha is one of the best, one of the best performers in the world. Not great with business and personal life she’s had all kinds of problems. It affected me and everybody else around her. Tragic-wise it’s something that you have to deal with if you’re going to deal with the person. Aretha to me has always been wonderful. I love her and to me I love her from a distance. Because when I have to run I’m going to be able to run and get away from her. But that’s something that’s personal and the business and the personal thing doesn’t quite work hand in hand with her. So you just have to know how to deal with it. Steely Dan? I didn’t have a problem. Steely Dan was one of the hardest groups in the world for me to work with, but I don’t have that problem of working with people. I leave them alone. I go in, I do my job, and I leave.
Well those guys are pretty controlling in the studio, is that right? That’s what I’ve heard.
Oh yes. But it’s like anything else, you do your job and that’s all they want. And it works. They’ll allow you to do what you do.
And they didn’t call you by accident, that’s for sure. Right?
I mean they wanted you in that seat.
But see I didn’t know — you go by the reputation of the things that you hear, even before all these things happening. And for me I said oh, okay. It didn’t matter. It didn’t matter

who the artist was as far as I’m concerned. An artist is an artist. You go in, you do your job, and you leave. Now if you’re lucky enough to socialize with them on the outside after the job is done, great, fine. But it is not a way of life. I enjoy the artists. I enjoy all the names. I enjoy all the unknown names. They pay me to come in to do a job. That’s what I’m going to do. I’m going to do the job, and I’m going to get out of your way. Now our paths cross further down the line it’s always going to be a very nice thing. Because it’s going to be the same. Talking about bad or something? What am I going to talk about that’s bad? What did we do that was so bad? I don’t know all the problems that you have of such and such and such. But you didn’t hurt me. And if you did hurt me, I’ll leave you alone. It’s that simple. I don’t have to go and really go through all the changes of being hurt again when I know that you’re going to hurt me. For what? For money? I can make money when I can’t do anything else. I know how to make money. But I am good at what I do which is what gives me the opportunity to make money. Hall & Oates, Simon & Garfunkel, Roberta Flack, Donnie Hathaway, everybody. When I really look at the overall picture I’ve had more fun than a barrel of monkeys. James Brown was a pain in the neck. When I had to do what I had to do to show my butt with him, I did it and it was over. You go in and you do your job. But that’s what it is for me. That’s how I was taught. That was the thing that was instilled in me first. If you don’t like it don’t accept it. You don’t do the job. I had to tell Barry Manilow — you want Steve Gadd? I’ll go call him. Hey, you don’t — don’t take me through these changes that, well you know you’re now — we’re big time Purdie so I said no, no. I was there when you were nothing. I was there when you were doing demos. That’s how far back I go with it. More power to you that you’re the biggest cheese out here. Wonderful. But like I said before don’t ask me to play like Steve Gadd. Because I am not Steve Gadd.
